risk.line: HIGH, held for a THIRTEENTH consecutive pass, and the evening closed both of Saudi Arabia's doors at once. Houthi forces took Perim Island at the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb, a day after taking Mokha and the Hanish Islands, leaving Yemen's Red Sea coastline held end to end according to four Yemeni government sources cited by Reuters; hours earlier the Saudi energy ministry confirmed it had shut the East-West crude pipeline - the 7 million barrel-a-day line built specifically to bypass Hormuz - as a precaution after attacks near Riyadh and Medina that caused injuries. The kingdom's eastern exit is under an Iranian permit regime and its western exit is now under Houthi guns and a closed valve. The dial does not move to CRIT on that, and saying so is the discipline: the published criterion is an American killed or a crewed American vessel hit, and neither happened. Two things argue against panic and are worth holding. The Houthi statement carves out everyone but Saudi vessels, which is a toll schedule rather than a blockade, and Windward's transit counts show inbound traffic holding at 13-17 while outbound thins - repricing, not closure. Against that, Mohammed bin Salman asked Trump twice on Thursday for strikes and was offered intelligence and targeting support instead, and the August CPI print landed at 3.4 per cent with gasoline up 27.4 per cent on the year and core beating forecast, moving September hike odds from 71 to 85 per cent. The war is now inside the inflation print.

forecasts.q: The President signs a determination or executive order invoking the Defense Production Act for petroleum REFINING capacity, before 31 Mar 2027
forecasts.note: OPENED at 55 today on a Reuters exclusive, and opened because this board has tracked the barrel, the strait and the pipeline for three weeks without ever writing a question on the thing that converts crude into the price a voter actually pays. FACTS, separated by class. CONFIRMED: Reuters, sourced to people familiar, reports the White House is weighing how to use the Defense Production Act to expand US refining capacity, and that the proposal came up at a recent meeting between the President and nearly a dozen refiners at which officials asked how federal support could best add capacity. CONFIRMED: the DPA, a 1950 Korean War statute, has never once been used to add refining capacity. REPORTED: refining executives told officials that federal money is better spent making existing plants more efficient or expanding them than financing a new refinery. The BASE RATE leads and it is why this opens above even money. Title III is not exotic - the Defense Department reported 4 active Title III projects in 1994, 37 in 2013 and 56 in 2024, and this administration already signed Executive Order 14241 for mineral production in March 2025. Administrations reported to be weighing a determination have generally signed one within months: baby formula in May 2022 came days after the political pressure, solar and grid components in June 2022 within weeks. The CONSTRAINT is the calendar - gasoline supplied more than a third of August's CPI increase and is up 27.4 per cent on the year, five weeks before a midterm. What holds this at 55 rather than 75 is the lawyers: refining is not obviously a material important to national defense in the sense Title III has been used, and the cheapest path for the White House is a DOE loan or grant announcement that looks identical on television and does NOT resolve this question yes. Kill: the midterms pass with no signed determination, or the administration announces refinery support explicitly under DOE authority instead, sends this to 20.

forecasts.q: Front-month Brent settles at or above $120/bbl on any daily settle before 31 Dec 2026
forecasts.note: RAISED 7, and the move is a VOLATILITY observation rather than a price one - which matters, because the mark six hours ago was CUT 7 on price. Spot barely moved: Brent is $104.91 late against the $104.53 marked this morning. What moved is the input that mark was computed ON. Brent traded a high of $110.19 today against a $97.92 prior close and a $103.48 low; a Parkinson estimate off that single range annualises to about 60 per cent, against the 35 to 45 per cent band this question's first-passage geometry has used since it opened. Recomputing with futures treated as driftless and a Broadie-Glasserman continuity correction for daily settlement monitoring gives 50 per cent at 45 per cent annualised volatility, 56 at 55 per cent and 59 at 60. The published method takes the conservative leg and trims two points for demand destruction and OPEC+ spare capacity, which lands on 52. One day's range is a noisy volatility estimate and today was the day a chokepoint changed hands, so the estimate is stated as noisy rather than dressed up - but a mark computed on 35 per cent volatility on a day the underlying moved 12 per cent intraday is a mark computed on the wrong number. Kill unchanged: ten consecutive settles below $95 sends this to 25.

forecasts.q: Dutch TTF front-month gas settles at or above EUR 100/MWh on any day before 31 Mar 2027
forecasts.note: OPENED at 42, paying the EUROPEAN GAS coverage debt this book first named on 2 September and has logged unpaid in two weekly audits since. The object is specific and the anchor is published. SPOT: TTF front-month is about EUR 73.55 a megawatt hour, up roughly 130 per cent this year, with month-ahead prices averaging near $21 per million BTU - the highest since December 2023 - and global LNG supply down more than 6 per cent year on year as Hormuz chokes Qatari and Emirati cargoes. European storage enters the last stretch of injection season below last year's level. GEOMETRY first: from EUR 73.55 the barrier is 30.7 per cent away in log terms with 201 days to run, and driftless first-passage with a daily-monitoring correction gives 41 per cent at 65 per cent annualised volatility and 46 at 75 - TTF has realised well above both in shock years. BASE RATE second, and it cuts the other way: of the last five European winters only two printed TTF above EUR 100, and both were winters with a live supply shock, which does describe this one. Opening two points below the geometry's mid because Europe's real adjustment mechanism is industrial demand destruction, which arrives before the price does and caps it. Kill: a Hormuz management arrangement that restarts Qatari LNG loadings, or a mild December with storage back above the five-year average, sends this to 15.

forecasts.q: Saudi Aramco or the Saudi authorities publicly confirm a force majeure at Yanbu, Jizan or Ras Tanura, OR a reduction in East-West (Petroline) pipeline throughput, before 31 Dec 2026
forecasts.note: RAISED 4 on the first hard third-party MEASUREMENT of the impairment this question is about. The IEA's September oil market report put Saudi crude supply at 6.0 million barrels a day in August, down 2.3 million on the month and the lowest in more than three decades, attributed to attacks on facilities and shipping routes; the agency cut its 2026 Saudi forecast by 885,000 barrels a day to 7.6 million and now expects global supply to fall 5.7 million this year against the 4.3 million it forecast a month ago. A quarter of a producer's output does not vanish without its buyers being told something, and that is the mechanism behind the raise. The CAP is the base rate, and it is the strongest counter-argument on this board: in September 2019 Abqaiq removed about 5.7 million barrels a day, more than twice today's loss, and Aramco did NOT declare force majeure - it delivered from storage and offered substitute grades to protect a reliability franchise worth more than any single cargo. The confirmation limb rises; the force-majeure limb does not. That is why this is 4 points and not 12. Kill unchanged: Aramco publishes normal Yanbu loading programmes through October and this goes to 15.

forecasts.q: The US ULSD (diesel) crack spread settles below $45/bbl on any daily settle before 15 Dec 2026
forecasts.note: RAISED 2 on a POLICY pathway that did not exist yesterday. The Reuters report that the White House is weighing the Defense Production Act for refining is not itself a crack-compressing event - new capacity takes years and cannot land inside this window - but it is direct evidence that the administration now treats the refining margin as a political object five weeks before a midterm, and the other tools in that drawer are fast. A refined-product export restriction, an SPR product release or a Jones Act waiver each compress the US crack within weeks by trapping supply onshore, and each has a precedent. Capped at 2 because the tool actually reported is capacity expansion, which is the slow one, and because the honest counter-mechanism still runs the other way: a crude-supply shock compresses the crack by raising the subtrahend, so part of the move this question needs could arrive for a reason that has nothing to do with policy. Kill: a US diesel export restriction announced, or Russian refinery runs restored, would take this above 45 quickly.

forecasts.q: The FOMC raises the fed funds target range at or before the 9-10 December 2026 meeting
forecasts.note: HELD at 72, and the hold is the most disciplined decision of the session. The ten-year jumped 19 basis points today to 4.97 and the thirty-year to 5.36, and the wires read it as the market pushing the Fed closer to a hike. That is the market repricing the SAME August CPI this book already spent 7 points on this morning - headline 3.4 per cent against a 3.3 consensus, core 0.3 per cent on the month against 0.2 expected, gasoline supplying more than a third of the monthly rise. Marking a bond move that is the echo of a print you have already marked is the double count this ledger keeps catching itself on, and the 6 September audit named this very question as the one that had failed to price its own counter-framework. It stays at 72 because that counterweight is unchanged: core CPI on the YEAR fell to 2.4 from 2.5, still the single number saying energy rather than general inflation, and Blinder and Bernanke's finding that central banks have generally been right to look through supply shocks has not been repealed by one month. The real test is Wednesday's statement language, not the rate.

forecasts.q: USD/JPY appreciates 8 per cent or more from its 3 Sep 2026 level (160.0 to 147.2 or below) within any rolling 30-day window, before 31 Mar 2027
forecasts.note: HELD at 31 with a clean data vintage for a second session. USD/JPY is 153.75 live against the 153.42 marked this morning - no move worth a point, and for once no gap to refuse on. The geometry is worth publishing because it explains why this is 31 and not 10: a SINGLE 30-day window from 153.75 to the 147.20 barrier is only about 17 per cent at 11 per cent annualised volatility, but the question allows any rolling window through March, and the barrier can be approached from a lower spot later in the period. Both legs of the August 2024 template fall inside the next week - the FOMC on the 16th and the Bank of Japan on the 18th, with a hike being priced after board member Hajime Takata said the bank should move nimbly. The published falsifier stands: a BoJ hold that sends the yen back through 158 cuts this to 18.

forecasts.q: Major US and/or Israeli strike campaign on Iran resumes (multi-day, state targets)
forecasts.note: HELD at 50. The President used the twenty-fifth anniversary of 11 September at the Pentagon to link the attacks to the war on Iran, and the Defense Secretary did the same. That is narrative, and Standing Order 3 governs: translate a speech into a desk, a statute or a flow, and discard the rest. There is no new desk here and no new flow. The revealed-preference fact that bought yesterday's cut is unchanged and it is the one that matters - the Saudi crown prince asked twice on Thursday for American strikes on the Houthis and was refused, with CENTCOM sending intelligence and targeting support instead, under a policy an administration official described as empowering regional partners to take the lead. A memorial address is the cheapest possible signal; a refused request from the closest regional partner is an expensive one.

forecasts.q: Saudi Arabia publicly announces enrichment, weapons pursuit, or a nuclear-sharing arrangement
forecasts.note: HELD at 18 after yesterday's raise on Sagan's security model - a client hedges when the credibility of its patron's guarantee falls, not when the threat rises. Both halves moved again today in the same directions: the threat is measurably worse, with Saudi output at a thirty-year low and the Red Sea exit declared hostile to Saudi hulls, while the American answer remains intelligence and targeting rather than strikes. No points are spent, because this question resolves on a Saudi ANNOUNCEMENT about enrichment, weapons or sharing, and nothing was announced. The pathway is logged for a third day; the points stay unspent until the variable matches.

HELD at 31. Israel's destruction of the Hezbollah subterranean complex on the Ali al-Taher ridge - a reported 1,000 tonnes of explosives, a tremor read at magnitude 4.1 - led the wires again today, and the framing that bought yesterday's cut is unchanged: Netanyahu and Katz described the operation as COMPLETING the consolidation of the security zone. Schelling's distinction governs. An operation publicised as consummating a limited objective is a price being banked, not a campaign being opened.

forecasts.q: Hormuz transits recover to more than 50 per cent of pre-war volume (about 65 a day against a 130 baseline)
forecasts.note: HELD at 10 for a SEVENTH instance of the same pattern, and the pattern is itself the finding. Iran's foreign ministry confirmed today that it will discuss the Strait of Hormuz with Gulf states on Monday in Salalah, and oil fell on it. This desk's standing rule is that an announcement is not a transit, and it has now been applied to Qatar's unconditional-reopening appeal, to the Beijing venue, to the Oman corridor and now to a dated ministerial meeting. The admissible evidence class is a transit count: seven on Wednesday against a ten-day average of 14, against the roughly 65 a day this question needs. The base rate is Suez, closed in June 1967 and reopened in June 1975, where clearance alone took about a year AFTER the political decision was taken.

hypotheses.name: IRGC captured the succession (weak form — assessed finding)
hypotheses.d: Documented pressure on Assembly electors, 8 boycotts, overridden shortlist and will. The pre-arranged-pact version scores only 30% — the plan was overridden, not executed.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Houthis seize Perim Island and Yemen's entire Red Sea coast
brief.h: Four Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi forces took Perim (Mayyun) on Friday after capturing Mokha and the Hanish Islands the day before, leaving the 20-kilometre narrows of the Bab el-Mandeb under their guns and Yemen's Red Sea coastline held end to end.
brief.t: The important thing here is not that a militia took an island. It is that the last unconstrained exit from the Red Sea now has an owner who charges by the flag. The Houthi statement said the operation was a success and that 'maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels' - which is not a promise of safety, it is a published tariff schedule with one name on it. Hold the sequencing: Hormuz went to a permit regime this summer, Saudi Arabia rerouted its barrels west to Yanbu and the Red Sea to escape it, and the west door has now been closed behind them. A Houthi official told Al Jazeera they did not even need the strait, 'for the blockade is already in place' - the honest version of the same point.
brief.context: The rail is the 2015 intervention and the four-year truce that collapsed in July; the offensive Yahya Saree dates to 3 September is the first Houthi campaign fought for coastline rather than for leverage over Riyadh. The deciding desk is not the Pentagon podium but the Lloyd's Joint War Committee and the war-risk underwriters, who convert a held island into a per-voyage price without anyone declaring anything. The base rate to keep: chokepoints are almost never closed, they are taxed - the Danish Sound Dues ran for four centuries on exactly this logic, and every modern episode from the Tanker War to the 2024 Red Sea campaign ended in selective transit, not closure. What would change the read is a non-Saudi hull hit, which converts a discriminatory toll into a general blockade. Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice on Thursday asking for strikes and was offered intelligence and targeting support instead, per CBS sources - that refusal is the load-bearing fact of the week.

angles.effect: GAIN the thing they have never had - a revenue-shaped instrument. A carve-out that exempts everyone but Saudi ships buys them the world's indifference while they strangle one customer
PAYS twice. Its eastern exit is under an Iranian permit regime and its western exit is now under Houthi guns, and it has been publicly refused the American strikes that would reopen either

GAIN in the narrow sense that war-risk premia reprice - a Red Sea transit was already running $1-2 million at 0.5-1 per cent of hull value - and PAY in the wider one, because a Cape of Good Hope reroute adds roughly ten days to Asia-Europe
PAYS with no seat at the table. Suez dues are a hard-currency line in the budget and every diverted hull is a fee that never arrives

dec.kill: A non-Saudi vessel struck or mined in the strait would kill the 'safe for all but one flag' read and make this a blockade. Conversely, thirty days of normal non-Saudi transits at a stable premium would confirm the toll read.

consp.claim: That this is the opening move of general war - that with a second strait closed and the Suez route behind it, oil goes to $500 and Europe goes dark this winter; and alongside it, the claim that the US is not failing to stop the Houthis but choosing not to, because a barefoot militia shutting down oil shipping is proof the American security guarantee was always a bluff.
consp.spread: A 271-reply /pol/ thread headed 'WW3 FUCKING IMMINENT' in full capitals, a 165-reply companion arguing America is a failed state, and the board's long-running Persia-Israel general, which lists the day's captures as more than 4,000 square kilometres taken in under 24 hours
consp.read: Two frames stacked: the catastrophist price-spiral and the hegemon-in-decline read. The checkable kernel in the second one is the strongest thing on the board today - MBS did ask, and was told no, and that refusal is sourced. The first frame fails on arithmetic: Bab el-Mandeb is a route, not a source, and a reroute adds days and dollars rather than removing barrels. The $500 number has no mechanism attached to it.

brief.head: Saudi Arabia shuts the pipeline built to bypass Hormuz
brief.h: The Saudi energy ministry said on Friday that the East-West crude line from Abqaiq to Yanbu - nameplate 7 million barrels a day, and the kingdom's designed escape from the Strait of Hormuz - was closed as a precautionary measure after multiple attacks on Thursday morning in the Riyadh and Medina regions that caused injuries.
brief.t: Follow the plumbing rather than the map. The East-West pipeline is not an export route among several; it is the single physical answer Saudi Arabia built to the question 'what if Hormuz closes'. Laid after the Tanker War, kept underused for decades at real cost, and pressed into heavy service this summer when Hormuz went to a permit regime, it was the reason Riyadh could still put crude on water while the Gulf exit was rationed. Shutting it as a precaution is the operationally correct decision and the strategically worst one: it means the kingdom has, for now, no unconstrained way out in either direction. That is the actual content of Friday - not damage, but the loss of optionality.
brief.context: The rail predates the crisis by forty years, which is what makes this readable rather than speculative: Saudi planners in the 1980s priced exactly this scenario and built steel against it. The deciding desk is Aramco's loading programme, not the energy ministry's statement - a published October schedule for Yanbu at normal volumes says this is a shipping interruption, continued silence says it is a production one. The base rate on infrastructure attacks is restoration in days to weeks: Abqaiq in 2019 took 5.7 million barrels a day offline and was substantially restored inside two and a half weeks. What breaks that base rate is not the size of the damage but the rate of repeat attacks, because a line cannot be repaired while it is being hit. Note the IEA already measured Saudi August output at 6.0 million barrels a day, down 2.3 million on the month and the lowest in more than three decades.

angles.effect: GAINS by the word 'precautionary'. It frames a shutdown as a choice rather than a consequence, which is true of the valve and says nothing about the steel

GAIN a claim far larger than their demonstrated damage - their own channels say the strike halted nearly 7 million barrels a day, which is the pipe's nameplate, not its throughput, and not a measured loss
PAY. The grades this line carries are the medium and heavy barrels that make diesel, and the US diesel print is already at a record
GAINS without firing. Every hour the western bypass is shut is an hour the Hormuz permit regime is the only door, which is the entire premise of its leverage

dec.kill: An Aramco force-majeure notice on Yanbu loadings would confirm this is a supply event. A restart announcement inside two weeks with October volumes unchanged would confirm it was a precaution that worked.

consp.claim: That the pipeline was destroyed at multiple points and that Saudi export capacity is effectively finished - the circulating version puts eight or more simultaneous rupture points along the line near Medina and reads the ministry's 'precautionary' wording as cover for catastrophic damage.
consp.spread: The /pol/ Persia-Israel general, which lists the strike as having halted nearly 7 million barrels a day, plus OSINT accounts on X circulating Sentinel imagery of smoke southeast of Medina and trade-press pickups of the same frames
consp.read: This is the 'the official number is always the floor' frame, and it has a real kernel: something did force an unplanned stoppage, and the ministry did confirm attacks and injuries. But the best instrument pointed at it cuts the other way - the Payne Institute's VIIRS Nightfire read found emergency flaring at flares that were already catalogued, and explicitly no new fires at previously uncatalogued locations, which is the signature of a line being depressurised in a hurry rather than of eight fresh holes in it.

brief.head: Gasoline drives August inflation and all but locks a Fed hike
brief.h: Headline CPI rose 0.4 per cent on the month and held at 3.4 per cent on the year, with gasoline up 3.9 per cent on the month and 27.4 per cent on the year doing more than a third of the work; core rose 0.3 per cent against a 0.2 per cent forecast, and futures moved from a 71 per cent chance of a September hike to 85 per cent.
brief.t: This is the print where a war becomes a domestic policy problem. The mechanism has a name - energy pass-through, the way a fuel shock migrates out of the energy line and into everything that has to be trucked - and the number that matters is not the 3.4 per cent headline but the core beat. A pure energy shock shows up in headline and leaves core alone; a central bank can look through that, and every one of them wants to. Core at 0.3 per cent against a 0.2 per cent forecast is the evidence that the shock has already started migrating, six days before the FOMC votes. That is why the odds jumped rather than drifted.
brief.context: The rail is the 1970s precedent every governor on the committee was trained on: the Fed looked through the first oil shock, watched it become wage-and-price inflation, and spent a decade paying for it. The deciding desk is the FOMC on 16 September, with the funds rate at 3.50-3.75 per cent where it has sat all year - a hike would be the first in more than three years. The base rate worth holding is that central banks tighten into energy shocks less often than the rhetoric suggests, because the shock is itself contractionary; the ECB dropping its look-through language last week is the signal that this cycle may be the exception. What would change the read is the core number - a 0.2 per cent core print next month takes the argument away, whatever gasoline does.

angles.effect: GAINS cover. A hot core print lets it move on credibility grounds rather than be seen responding to a war, which is the framing it needs going into a midterm
PAYS directly. It is refinancing into a tightening cycle with the thirty-year already at 5.36 per cent, and this week's buyback attempt did not move it
PAY twice - 27.4 per cent more for gasoline on the year, and a higher policy rate on top of it, which is the part of the mechanism no announcement softens
PAYS politically and GAINS an argument. A rate hike five weeks before a midterm is a bad headline; an energy-driven print is also the strongest case it has for the refining measures it is shopping

dec.kill: A hold on 16 September with a statement that keeps look-through language would kill the 'pass-through has begun' read. A hike plus removal of that language confirms it.

consp.claim: That the inflation number is downstream of a deliberate policy rather than of a war - the circulating versions run from 'oil is actually running out and the market is only now admitting it' to a claim that a $5,000-per-adult pre-election payment amounting to $1.5 trillion is being prepared, to the simpler charge that the economy is being wrecked on purpose.
consp.spread: A 107-reply /biz/ thread on the record diesel print, an 82-reply thread on the $5,000 claim built around a viral X post, a 53-reply thread on a Cramer clip predicting $150 oil, and a 74-reply thread asking why the president is 'actively trying to destroy the country financially'
consp.read: Scarcity-by-design plus the pre-election-bribe frame, held simultaneously despite pointing opposite ways. The kernel is the price itself - gasoline really is up 27.4 per cent and diesel really did set a record. Both frames fail on the same point: an administration engineering dear fuel would not be absorbing record pump prices five weeks before a midterm.

brief.head: Putin presses BRICS to counter the West on his Delhi visit
brief.h: Putin and Modi held a bilateral on the eve of the Delhi summit, with the Kremlin's Dmitry Peskov saying the two sides are discussing a BrahMos upgrade and remain committed to completing S-400 deliveries, while Putin insisted the grouping 'is not against anyone' and attacked Western economic restrictions.
brief.t: The two sentences Putin said on Friday are the whole story: BRICS is not against anyone, and Western restrictions are illegitimate. Those are not in tension, they are the product on offer - a bloc that supplies sanctions insulation while disclaiming that it is a bloc. India is the perfect venue for it because India will not buy the political version and will buy the commercial one: discounted crude, missile co-production, a settlement channel it can use without signing anything. Watch what gets named in the declaration tomorrow, because a named instrument with capital and a date behind it is a different object from an eighteenth communique about multipolarity.
brief.context: The rail is the post-2022 payments workaround built out of rupee-rouble accounts, dirham settlement and Chinese CIPS messaging - improvised plumbing that has moved real oil without ever becoming a system. The deciding desk is not the summit hall but Indian bank compliance departments and the correspondent banks in New York and Frankfurt that clear their dollar legs; those desks have quietly killed more BRICS settlement schemes than any Western statement. The base rate is unforgiving: every summit since 2009 has produced the aspiration and none has produced the instrument. What would change it is a document naming a facility with a size, a currency and a start date - not a paragraph welcoming local-currency trade.

angles.effect: GAINS the photograph. Being received in Delhi alongside Xi, Pezeshkian, Ramaphosa and MBZ is the refutation of isolation, and it costs Moscow nothing to supply

GAINS on both sides of the ledger - discounted barrels and weapons co-production from Moscow while keeping its US technology and defence relationships, which is why it will resist any language that forces a choice
GAINS if the bloc institutionalises, because the settlement rails on offer are overwhelmingly its own; it PAYS if the summit ends in aspiration, which flatters Delhi's hosting and builds nothing
PAY slowly. Each workaround that clears without penalty lowers the expected cost of the next one, and that erosion is cumulative rather than dramatic

dec.kill: A declaration naming a settlement instrument with capital and a start date would break an eighteen-summit base rate. A declaration that only welcomes local-currency trade confirms it.

consp.claim: That the real object of the Ukraine war was always the European gas market - that Europe was made to replace Russian pipeline gas with American LNG and now pays roughly twelve times what US consumers pay, and that this transfer, not the battlefield, is the point.
consp.spread: A 124-reply /pol/ thread built on a viral X post comparing the two gas prices, recycled through the board's Ukraine generals
consp.read: The pipeline-is-the-real-reason frame, and the kernel is a real price gap: European TTF gas does trade at a large multiple of US Henry Hub, and US LNG did take the share Russian pipe gas lost. The frame skips the mechanism - the spread is mostly liquefaction, shipping and regasification cost plus scarcity rent, and it existed before 2022 - and it treats a consequence American exporters profited from as proof of the intention behind the invasion.

brief.head: Brazil unseals a corruption probe into Lula's main challenger
brief.h: Brazil's Supreme Court unsealed documents showing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing candidate against Lula in next month's election, is under investigation for allegedly receiving 61 million reais - about $12 million - from Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro to finance a film about his father, with the probe opened in July by Justice Andre Mendonca.
brief.t: The detail that carries the analysis is who opened it. Andre Mendonca is a Bolsonaro appointee, recently celebrated on the Brazilian right and by Flavio Bolsonaro himself - which removes the cleanest available defence, that this is a hostile court running a lawfare operation before a vote. What is left is the Banco Master collapse doing what failed banks always do, which is to make every payment the institution ever sent discoverable at once. The timing question is real and separate: a probe opened in July and unsealed in September, with polls showing a statistical tie in a simulated runoff, is a decision about disclosure, and disclosure decisions have authors.
brief.context: The rail is Lava Jato and the machinery it left behind - a Supreme Court with direct jurisdiction over sitting politicians, a plea-bargain regime, and two decades of Brazilian elections in which the bank ledger rather than the campaign decides who runs. The deciding desk is the Supreme Court's first panel and the central bank's resolution of Banco Master, which is where the underlying documents come from. The base rate matters: in Brazil, unsealed investigations into presidential candidates land far more often than they disqualify, and their measured effect on vote share has repeatedly been smaller than the coverage implies - Lula's own conviction and later annulment is the extreme case. What would change this read is an indictment rather than an investigation, because only the former starts a clock that can collide with the electoral calendar.

angles.effect: GAINS a week of coverage it did not have to buy, in a race polls put at a statistical tie in the second round
PAYS in headlines and GAINS a grievance that has already worked once in this family - though the appointing judge being his own side's makes the persecution frame harder to run
PAYS institutional credibility either way. Acting close to a vote invites the lawfare charge; sitting on unsealed evidence invites the cover-up charge

angles.party: Banco Master's depositors and the resolution authority
angles.effect: PAY, and are absent from the coverage - the failed bank is the reason any of these documents exist

dec.kill: A formal indictment before the first round would make this an electoral event rather than a news cycle. The race closing again in polls within two weeks would confirm the base rate.

watch: An Aramco force-majeure notice on Yanbu loadings, or the absence of one. That single document is the difference between a shipping interruption and a production loss, and it settles the East-West pipeline story faster than any statement from the energy ministry.

The first non-Saudi hull hit or mined in the Bab el-Mandeb. The Houthi carve-out - safe for all companies except Saudi vessels - is the entire reason this is a toll rather than a blockade, and one wrong target ends that distinction permanently.

Whether Washington moves from intelligence and targeting support to strikes on Houthi positions. MBS asked twice on Thursday and was refused; a reversal inside a week would say the refusal was a bargaining position, and continued refusal says the security guarantee now has published limits.

The FOMC statement on Wednesday, specifically the sentence about energy rather than the rate. With a hike priced at 85 per cent, the decision is already in the market - whether look-through language survives is the part that is not.

Whether tomorrow's BRICS declaration in Delhi names an instrument with a size, a currency and a start date. Eighteen summits have produced eighteen aspirations, and that base rate stands until a document breaks it.
lesson: Here is a piece of history that explains three of today's stories at once. In 1973 the Arab oil embargo taught America that it could be starved of crude, and Congress answered in 1975 with the Energy Policy and Conservation Act: it built the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, a salt-cavern hoard of crude on the Gulf Coast, and banned the export of American crude for forty years. It was a serious, expensive, well-designed answer to the wrong half of the problem. America insured the ROCK and never insured the FACTORY - no major new US refinery has been built since 1977, and refining is where crude becomes the diesel that moves freight and the gasoline that shows up in an inflation print. The mechanism to keep is Albert Hirschman's, from his 1945 study of trade and power: dependence is not measured by how much you import, it is measured by how costly it is for you to SWITCH. Crude is fungible and switchable - grades differ, but a cargo is a cargo. Conversion capacity is not switchable at all; you cannot import a distillation tower in a hurry, and you cannot build one in less than about five years. So the country that controls conversion, not the country that owns the reservoir, sets the price that voters feel. That is why Russia's gasoline export ban, a burned refinery at Jazan, a drone fire at Saratov and a White House meeting about a 1950 statute are one story rather than four - and it predicts something specific and checkable: through this winter, watch crack spreads and product export restrictions rather than crude, because the scarce thing is the tower. The honest caveat is that Hirschman's framework tells you where the leverage sits and not how long it lasts; refining margins have collapsed from records before, and the fastest way this whole picture breaks is a demand recession, which fixes the shortage by destroying the customer.

events.label: Brownsville, Texas
events.note: Site of the 168,000 b/d America First Refining project announced in March - the first new US refinery in nearly 50 years - and the reference point in the White House's Defense Production Act discussions.

events.label: Washington
events.note: The FOMC meets 16 September after August CPI of 3.4 per cent with core accelerating; Treasury's upsized buyback failed again as the 30-year hit 5.36 per cent.

events.label: Saratov
events.note: Ukrainian drones started a fire at the Rosneft refinery overnight. Russia's gasoline export suspension, imposed 27 August after earlier strikes, runs to 30 September.

events.label: Perim (Bab el-Mandeb)
events.note: Houthi forces hold the island that splits the strait at its narrowest point, completing control of Yemen's western coast. The UAE-built runway on it is the emplacement tripwire.

events.label: Mocha
events.note: The Red Sea port fell on 10 September. The UN reports at least 46,000 people displaced by the escalating fighting along the coast.

events.label: Yanbu
events.note: Red Sea terminus of the East-West pipeline and the loading point for barrels that avoid Hormuz. An October loading programme, or its absence, is the real signal behind GEO-032.

events.label: Jazan
events.note: The 400,000 b/d refinery, roughly a tenth of Aramco's net refining, hit or shut three times since late July. Part of why Saudi supply printed a thirty-year low.

events.label: Strait of Hormuz
events.note: Seven transits on Wednesday against a ten-day average of 14 and a pre-war baseline near 130 a day. The Iranian permit regime remains in force.

events.label: Salalah

quiz.q: Today's brief argues the world is short refining rather than short crude. What is the mechanism that makes that distinction matter?
options: Crude can be substituted between grades fairly easily, but conversion capacity cannot be imported or built quickly, so whoever controls refining sets the price consumers feel
Crude reserves are running out globally while refineries are abundant
Refineries are cheaper to build than oil wells, so they are always the first bottleneck
Oil producers have agreed to cut crude output in order to protect refining margins
quiz.why: This is Hirschman's switching-cost idea: dependence is about how costly it is to switch, not how much you import. A cargo of crude has substitutes; a distillation tower takes about five years and cannot be shipped.

quiz.q: Why does this desk treat the Treasury's bond buyback as unlikely to lower long-term yields on its own?
options: Because buybacks are illegal without Congressional approval
Because a buyback changes the composition of the debt but not its quantity - Treasury must issue something else to fund it
Because the Federal Reserve has publicly opposed the programme
Because foreign investors are legally barred from participating in buyback operations
quiz.why: Retiring a long bond requires issuing shorter debt to pay for it. That is a maturity swap, not a reduction in borrowing, and the closest analogue - the 2022 gilt crisis - was stopped by a central bank buying, not by a debt office reshuffling.

quiz.q: The IEA reported Saudi crude supply at a thirty-year low. Why does the brief argue Aramco may still say nothing about it?
options: Saudi law prohibits disclosure of production figures
The IEA report already satisfies any disclosure obligation Aramco has
Aramco's core asset is a reliability franchise - the belief that its cargoes always arrive - and in 2019 it absorbed a larger outage at Abqaiq without ever declaring force majeure
Aramco has no contracts that require it to notify buyers of supply problems
quiz.why: The Abqaiq precedent is the base rate. A bigger outage produced no public admission because the franchise is worth more than any single cargo - which is why this board's scored question resolves on a document, not a satellite image.

quiz.q: What does the brief identify as Europe's actual adjustment mechanism when LNG cargoes get scarce?
options: Government rationing of household heating
Emergency restart of Russian pipeline contracts
Industrial demand destruction - the price rises until fertiliser, chemical or metals plants shut down
Drawing on a European strategic gas reserve
quiz.why: In a global auction Europe cannot make more gas appear; it can only bid until some buyer stops. The industrial buyer stops first, which is why ammonia and chlorine lines go before household bills move.

quiz.q: CRITICAL THINKING. A post argues: 'American oil producers are making record profits from a strait closed at both ends - that tells you who arranged it.' What is the flaw, and what observable would test the claim?
options: No flaw; profit is the strongest available evidence of who caused an event

The flaw is treating benefit as evidence of authorship. A test would be whether the same actors are bearing costs they would have avoided - such as an administration absorbing record pump prices five weeks before an election
The flaw is that oil producers do not actually profit from high prices
The flaw is that the strait is not closed at both ends, so the premise is simply false
quiz.why: Asking who benefits is compulsory; concluding they must have caused it is the cui bono fallacy, because benefit sits downstream of an event and almost everything benefits somebody. The test is to look for costs the supposed author would never have chosen to pay.

plumbing.epoch: E6, the 2008-2022 quantitative-easing rail in its unwind chapter, meeting E4, the 1973 security-for-barrels bargain - and today E4 was the one that moved. That bargain traded American security guarantees for dollar-priced oil, and its unstated assumption was that the guarantor would keep the sea lanes open and would show up when a client was attacked. Both halves of that assumption were tested in one day: a chokepoint changed hands, a fire burned over the only pipeline that routes around the other chokepoint, and the guarantor declined a treaty partner's direct request for strikes, offering intelligence and targeting data instead. The old rail: a security guarantee underwritten by a navy with forward basing. The new permit: the guarantee is now explicitly partial - freedom of navigation for the lane, but the land war behind it is the partner's problem - and that repricing is happening at the same moment the monetary half of the bargain is being asked to absorb a supply shock with a demand instrument.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
